subject: Humanities
objective_verbatim: Why we remember: significance of remembrance.
focus: Explain the significance of remembrance through people, warning and responsibility; compare generic forms and write a structured answer.

source_workbook.basis: Owner brief: LAUNCH Weekly Spring row 43. Workbook not re-read; inherited workbook provenance is retained for traceability only.

assessment_generic: Formative historical explanation. Assess reasons and understanding, not an emotional display, ritual, pledge or public performance. No accredited completion inferred.

Supported: Use R1–R3 to name the people, the warning and the responsibility. An adult may read exactly; choose a reason for each purpose.
Use R4, R5 or R6 as your example. Say how that type serves a purpose. Keep the national day’s date and purpose from R5.
Use the frame for your own short answer. Include a limit and one safe responsibility. Point, type or direct a scribe if needed.
Independent: Explain the three purposes using R1–R3. Use one type from R4–R6 and explain how it helps.
Include the national day’s date and purpose. Show why learning and responsibility continue beyond a ceremony or a date.
Write your own structured answer with card codes, reasons, a limit and one safe responsibility today.
Aspire: Keep the same common finish. Explain how one type of remembrance could serve more than one purpose.
Compare the value and limits of two types without ranking communities or suffering. Explain why accurate context matters.
Make a reasoned judgement about why remembrance matters today. Avoid claiming that remembrance alone guarantees prevention.

sensitive_response_route: Point to PAUSE or tell the adult quietly. Use the agreed supervised place. You do not need to explain to the group. When ready, choose a private recap or more time with the quiet task. The adult will help you rejoin.
quiet_alternative: Quiet task: put these made-up daily times in order: 14:00 club; 08:30 reading; 12:00 lunch; 10:00 break. Copy or point to the first and last. Then sort pencil and book, cup and plate, by use. No history words or personal story are needed.
staff_care_rules: This lesson is complete with the supplied text. Add no imagery or survivor testimony in any form: no quotation, paraphrase, invented voice, composite, audio, video or unplanned live browsing. The school’s chosen memorial-day resource may be reviewed privately by the teacher if the school approves, within the same care limits. No title, organisation or address is named here; no extra content is required.

Keep the dignity and full lives of people in view. Do not use imagine-you-are tasks, victim roles, historical role play, comparisons of suffering or personal family-history questions. Do not ask any learner to speak for Jewish people, survivors or a whole community. Do not invent a life story to make the topic feel personal.

Participation is thoughtful learning, not a performance of grief. Do not require a particular feeling, silence, prayer, pledge, public statement or personal disclosure. Quiet listening, private work and passing are allowed. Assess the explanation, not visible sadness or agreement with a ritual.

Agree a discreet PAUSE signal, supervising adult, quiet place and private return check before teaching. Keep both learners supervised. If a sole adult cannot supervise separate spaces, use a calm place in the room or pause the whole group while seeking usual support. Never send a learner away alone.

For distress, stop the demand, acknowledge it calmly and offer the agreed route without sanction or a public explanation. Do not probe or insist on a history recap while the learner is upset. Follow the school’s existing safeguarding arrangements for disclosures and use the appropriate private record.

Interrupt antisemitism calmly and firmly. Name the harm without repeating a slur. Hostility towards Jewish people is unacceptable. Correct a falsehood briefly and follow school procedures. Do not debate Holocaust denial or require learners to defend victims’ rights. Victims were not responsible for their persecution.

For flippancy or laughter, stop and reset respectful listening. A nervous response is possible, but harm still needs addressing. Follow up privately, check those affected and use existing procedures for targeted, repeated or serious incidents. Avoid shaming or guessing motives.

A warning is a reason to learn and act carefully, not a prediction that every unfair act leads to genocide. Do not equate everyday disagreement with the Holocaust. Remembrance alone cannot prevent hatred; education, laws, institutions and human choices matter too. Learners do not carry personal responsibility for preventing genocide.

Offer the neutral quiet task and a private readiness check. It is not evidence of the remembrance outcome. Record deferred work honestly and offer a later supported return. A partner’s answer or participation in a ceremony does not establish the learner’s understanding.
context: Remembrance means taking time to remember people and learn about the past. In this lesson we consider the people, the warning and the responsibility today. The Holocaust was the Nazi-led persecution and murder of six million European Jews. Other people also faced Nazi persecution and murder. Their experiences were not all the same.
source_card_status: These six cards are new teaching explanations. They describe purposes and types of remembrance. No person’s testimony, story, words or image is reproduced, paraphrased or invented.

source_cards.title: Remembering the people
source_cards.label: Purpose of remembrance
source_cards.body: People who were persecuted and murdered had full lives, identities, interests, families and communities. Remembrance can honour those lives and the loss to people and communities. It helps us see people as individuals, not only as a number.
source_cards.link: We can keep people’s dignity without inventing their words, feelings or life stories.
source_cards.think: Why does learning about lives matter as well as knowing a number?

source_cards.title: Learning from a warning
source_cards.label: Purpose of remembrance
source_cards.body: Careful study can show how prejudice, unfair rules and human choices caused harm. Remembering can help us recognise hatred and exclusion and question false claims. Events were not inevitable. People made decisions.
source_cards.link: A warning invites learning and care. It does not mean that every present-day disagreement is the same as the Holocaust.
source_cards.think: How can learning about the past help people judge a claim today?

source_cards.title: Responsibility today
source_cards.label: Purpose of remembrance
source_cards.body: Remembering can prompt us to learn accurately, treat people with dignity and check claims before sharing them. We can seek trusted adult help if we encounter antisemitism or targeted abuse. We do not have to confront someone or put ourselves at risk.
source_cards.link: A ceremony alone cannot stop hatred. Responsibility continues beyond one day and is shared across society.
source_cards.think: Name a safe responsibility that follows from learning, without making a personal pledge.

source_cards.title: Memorial places and objects
source_cards.label: One type of remembrance
source_cards.body: A memorial may be a place or object set aside to remember people and events. Names or clear information can help people learn and reflect. Some memorials are used for gatherings; others allow private reflection. Their design and use differ.
source_cards.link: A memorial needs context. One object cannot explain a whole history, and communities do not all remember in the same way.
source_cards.think: How could a memorial serve the purpose in R1? What else would help people learn?

source_cards.title: A shared day of remembrance
source_cards.label: One type of remembrance
source_cards.body: Holocaust Memorial Day is marked in the UK on 27 January each year. It remembers those murdered in the Holocaust, other victims of Nazi persecution and people murdered in later genocides. It offers time to learn and reflect on prejudice and hatred today. Our lesson is on 26 January, the day before.
source_cards.link: A shared day can create time for public or private remembrance. It does not require everyone to feel the same way or take part in one ritual. Learning can continue beyond that date.
source_cards.think: What is the national day for, and why is one day not enough on its own?

source_cards.title: Education and reflection
source_cards.label: One type of remembrance
source_cards.body: Lessons, talks, discussion and carefully checked historical records can help later generations learn. Education can explain people’s lives, decisions and the effects of persecution. It can help us challenge false claims and think about responsibility.
source_cards.link: Learning needs accurate facts, context and care. Communities may use religious or non-religious forms of remembrance. Practices vary within communities as well as between them.
source_cards.think: How could education support more than one purpose of remembrance?

purpose_and_care_checks.kind: Sensitive history and remembrance teaching guidance
purpose_and_care_checks.scope: Dignity, accurate context, full lives, no simulations or comparisons of suffering, thoughtful participation and careful present-day responsibility. Owner care rules take precedence. Checked outside this distributable pack.

national_day_general: Holocaust Memorial Day is marked in the UK on 27 January each year. It remembers those murdered in the Holocaust, other victims of Nazi persecution and people murdered in later genocides. It offers time to learn and reflect on prejudice and hatred today. Our lesson is on 26 January, the day before.
model: Remembering matters because people who were murdered should not be reduced to a number (R1). Education can explain how prejudice and choices caused harm (R2/R6). This can help people check false claims and seek safe help. A memorial may name people, while a shared day creates time to learn (R4/R5). However, a ceremony alone cannot stop hatred. Responsibility continues in careful speech, checking facts and safe reporting routes (R3).
success_criteria: Link a remembrance type to a purpose with a reason.
Give a structured answer with a limit and safe responsibility today.

hinge.question: Which best explains remembrance? A: One ceremony stops hatred for good. B: It helps honour people and learn from history, while responsibility continues. C: Everyone must feel the same sadness.
hinge.answer_and_decision_rule: B. A gives a guarantee that remembrance cannot provide. C wrongly requires one emotional response. Check both learners privately for a reason. If needed, model purpose versus guarantee, then use the parallel check before independent work.
hinge.parallel: A memorial contains names. Does it explain the whole history on its own? No. Names can honour individuals, but accurate context and education are also needed. Ask the learner to link the form to a purpose and name a limit.

pair_work: Purpose Finder locates a purpose; Reason Builder explains how a remembrance form supports it. Swap learning roles. A form may serve several purposes with a reason. Keep each learner’s own response.

evidence.common_finish: In your book, answer: Why does remembering matter today? Explain the people, the warning and the responsibility. Use one remembrance type and say how it serves a purpose. Include the national day’s date and purpose, one limit, and one safe responsibility today. Keep card codes and your own reasons.

resources.Shared_Resources/Vocabulary_Mat_White.do:
Words for remembrance and responsibility
Tuesday 26 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 4 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W04
White paper version. Read quietly, point, write, type, speak privately or direct a scribe. You may pass. No public answer or reading aloud is required.
Word
Meaning
remembrance
Taking time to remember people and learn about the past.
significance
Why something matters, including its effects and meaning.
dignity
The worth of each person and the respect they should receive.
memorial
A place or object set aside to remember people or events.
commemoration
An act or event that marks people or events from the past.
prejudice
An unfair judgement about a person or group.
antisemitism
Prejudice, hostility or hate directed at Jewish people.
persecution
Unfair and harmful treatment aimed at a group of people.
genocide
An attempt to destroy all or part of a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
responsibility
What people and society should do with care for others.
context
Information that helps us understand a fact or event.
limit
What an action cannot achieve on its own.
Say or point to a word for private help. No reading aloud is required.
Keep people’s dignity. Explain a reason rather than guessing another person’s feelings.

These six cards are new teaching explanations. They describe purposes and types of remembrance. No person’s testimony, story, words or image is reproduced, paraphrased or invented.
R1 Remembering the people
Purpose of remembrance
People who were persecuted and murdered had full lives, identities, interests, families and communities. Remembrance can honour those lives and the loss to people and communities. It helps us see people as individuals, not only as a number.
We can keep people’s dignity without inventing their words, feelings or life stories.
Think: Why does learning about lives matter as well as knowing a number?
R2 Learning from a warning
Purpose of remembrance
Careful study can show how prejudice, unfair rules and human choices caused harm. Remembering can help us recognise hatred and exclusion and question false claims. Events were not inevitable. People made decisions.
A warning invites learning and care. It does not mean that every present-day disagreement is the same as the Holocaust.
Think: How can learning about the past help people judge a claim today?
Purposes and forms of remembrance
Tuesday 26 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 4 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W04
Pink paper version. Read quietly, point, write, type, speak privately or direct a scribe. You may pass. No public answer or reading aloud is required.
R3 Responsibility today
Purpose of remembrance
Remembering can prompt us to learn accurately, treat people with dignity and check claims before sharing them. We can seek trusted adult help if we encounter antisemitism or targeted abuse. We do not have to confront someone or put ourselves at risk.
A ceremony alone cannot stop hatred. Responsibility continues beyond one day and is shared across society.
Think: Name a safe responsibility that follows from learning, without making a personal pledge.
R4 Memorial places and objects
One type of remembrance
A memorial may be a place or object set aside to remember people and events. Names or clear information can help people learn and reflect. Some memorials are used for gatherings; others allow private reflection. Their design and use differ.
A memorial needs context. One object cannot explain a whole history, and communities do not all remember in the same way.
Think: How could a memorial serve the purpose in R1? What else would help people learn?
Purposes and forms of remembrance
Tuesday 26 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 4 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W04
Pink paper version. Read quietly, point, write, type, speak privately or direct a scribe. You may pass. No public answer or reading aloud is required.
R5 A shared day of remembrance
One type of remembrance
Holocaust Memorial Day is marked in the UK on 27 January each year. It remembers those murdered in the Holocaust, other victims of Nazi persecution and people murdered in later genocides. It offers time to learn and reflect on prejudice and hatred today. Our lesson is on 26 January, the day before.
A shared day can create time for public or private remembrance. It does not require everyone to feel the same way or take part in one ritual. Learning can continue beyond that date.
Think: What is the national day for, and why is one day not enough on its own?
R6 Education and reflection
One type of remembrance
Lessons, talks, discussion and carefully checked historical records can help later generations learn. Education can explain people’s lives, decisions and the effects of persecution. It can help us challenge false claims and think about responsibility.
Learning needs accurate facts, context and care. Communities may use religious or non-religious forms of remembrance. Practices vary within communities as well as between them.
Think: How could education support more than one purpose of remembrance?

slides.title: Why we remember

shapes.name: outcome
shapes.text: Why we remember: significance of remembrance.

shapes.name: scope
shapes.text: Who do we remember? What can we learn? How can we act with care?

slides.notes:
Owner brief: LAUNCH Weekly Spring row 43. Tuesday 26 January 2027, P2, 40 minutes. Exact outcome: Why we remember: significance of remembrance.
Enquiry: Why does remembering matter today? The lesson precedes Holocaust Memorial Day on 27 January.
Remembrance means taking time to remember people and learn about the past. In this lesson we consider the people, the warning and the responsibility today. The Holocaust was the Nazi-led persecution and murder of six million European Jews. Other people also faced Nazi persecution and murder. Their experiences were not all the same.
All explanations are newly written. No survivor testimony, imagery, named organisation, website or copied memorial text is supplied.

slides.title: A calm way to take part
slides.stage: Calm preview, choices and supervised pause.

shapes.name: stage-title
shapes.text: A calm way to take part

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: You may pass, read quietly, point, write or speak privately.

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: We discuss remembrance through short explanations.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: No imagery or survivor testimony is in this pack.

shapes.name: body-3
shapes.text: PAUSE: signal the adult. Use the agreed supervised place.

slides.notes:
Point to PAUSE or tell the adult quietly. Use the agreed supervised place. You do not need to explain to the group. When ready, choose a private recap or more time with the quiet task. The adult will help you rejoin.
Quiet task: put these made-up daily times in order: 14:00 club; 08:30 reading; 12:00 lunch; 10:00 break. Copy or point to the first and last. Then sort pencil and book, cup and plate, by use. No history words or personal story are needed.
Preview the lesson quietly if helpful. No one must show an emotion, disclose family history, speak for a community, read aloud or take part in a public act. A calm factual answer is valid. Agree supervision before teaching and retain the private return route.

slides.title: What remembrance means
slides.stage: Retrieve dignity and careful learning; define remembrance without personal disclosure.

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: Remembrance gives time to remember people and learn about the past.

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: People had full lives, relationships, interests and hopes.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: A respectful answer can be calm and factual.

shapes.name: body-3
shapes.text: No one has to show grief, share a personal story or join a public act.

slides.notes: Remembrance can remember individual lives, support historical learning and prompt responsibility. Avoid reducing people to how they were harmed. Do not invent a biography, voice or survivor experience to illustrate this point. Invite an idea about what remembrance is for, with passing available. This is a knowledge and explanation task, not a test of grief.

slides.title: Purposes of remembrance
slides.stage: Three purposes: people, warning and responsibility.

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: R1 People: keep individual lives and dignity in view.

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: R2 Warning: learn how hatred, unfair rules and choices caused harm.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: R3 Responsibility: check facts and respond safely to hatred today.

shapes.name: distinction
shapes.text: Remembrance can support care. It cannot guarantee that harm will never happen.

slides.notes: Use the three purposes as linked ways to explain significance, rather than a ritual or a promise that remembrance alone prevents harm. Warning concerns learning how prejudice, unjust rules and human choices caused harm. Responsibility includes checking claims, respecting dignity and seeking safe adult help for hatred. No comparison of suffering or claim that everyday disagreement is the same as the Holocaust. Use the explanatory cards and professional care notes recorded in SOURCE_MANIFEST.json without naming organisations or websites.

slides.title: An answer with a reason
slides.stage: Model a purpose-to-example reason; fade a link and check both learners privately.

shapes.name: model-label
shapes.text: Teacher-written explanation only. No historical person is quoted.

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: Remembering keeps people’s lives in view, beyond how they were harmed.

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: Learning about the past can help us recognise hatred and unfair treatment.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: This matters today because we can check facts and seek safe adult help.

slides.notes:
Remembering matters because people who were murdered should not be reduced to a number (R1). Education can explain how prejudice and choices caused harm (R2/R6). This can help people check false claims and seek safe help. A memorial may name people, while a shared day creates time to learn (R4/R5). However, a ceremony alone cannot stop hatred. Responsibility continues in careful speech, checking facts and safe reporting routes (R3).
Fade the completed answer and ask privately for a reason linking a purpose to why remembrance matters. Read exact words as access; record reasoning prompts separately. The model is a teacher-written explanation with no testimony or invented historical voice. It is not a required personal feeling or pledge.

slides.title: Forms of remembrance
slides.stage: Compare memorials, shared days and education; hinge and parallel check.

shapes.name: table-question
shapes.text: How can a form of remembrance serve a purpose? What else does it need?

tables: A place to pause and remember
People can choose how to take part
slides.notes:
Compare forms by what they can help people do, not by ranking communities or claiming that one form suits everyone. A memorial may provide a place to pause but needs context. A day can focus learning, which should continue beyond that date. Education needs accurate evidence and respectful choices. Some forms are religious, some are not. No named organisation, memorial or website is needed.
Which best explains remembrance? A: One ceremony stops hatred for good. B: It helps honour people and learn from history, while responsibility continues. C: Everyone must feel the same sadness.
B. A gives a guarantee that remembrance cannot provide. C wrongly requires one emotional response. Check both learners privately for a reason. If needed, model purpose versus guarantee, then use the parallel check before independent work.
A memorial contains names. Does it explain the whole history on its own? No. Names can honour individuals, but accurate context and education are also needed. Ask the learner to link the form to a purpose and name a limit.

slides.title: Reasons and respectful choices
slides.stage: Purpose Finder and Reason Builder connect forms to purposes, swap and explain a limit.

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: Use R4–R6: choose a memorial, a shared day or education.

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: Explain how it can help remember people, warn or guide responsibility.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: Different communities and individuals may choose different forms.

shapes.name: body-3
shapes.text: Listen, build on a reason or disagree kindly. Passing is allowed.

slides.notes: Seven minutes of paired discussion. Use the learning roles supplied in the print pack and swap roles. Each learner should offer or select a reason, or pass; a partner’s response is not both learners’ understanding. Ask how one form serves a purpose and what its limits are. Different communities and individuals choose different forms. Do not require a ritual, minute of silence, pledge or personal disclosure. Use the hinge and parallel check if they have not yet been completed. Keep the no-imagery and no-testimony boundary throughout.

slides.title: Your own structured answer
slides.stage: Each learner writes a structured answer with frame, codes, national-day purpose and a limit.

shapes.name: task-main
shapes.text: Why does remembering matter today? Keep three purposes, one form, the day’s date and purpose, a limit and safe responsibility.

shapes.name: route-body-0
shapes.text:
Use one idea at a time.
Choose a frame.
Explain why it matters.

shapes.name: route-body-1
shapes.text:
Link purposes to reasons.
Use a form as an example.
Keep a clear limit.

shapes.name: route-body-2
shapes.text:
Keep the common finish.
Weigh what a form can do.
Explain a limit with care.

slides.notes:
In your book, answer: Why does remembering matter today? Explain the people, the warning and the responsibility. Use one remembrance type and say how it serves a purpose. Include the national day’s date and purpose, one limit, and one safe responsibility today. Keep card codes and your own reasons.
Remembering matters because ____. First, it honours people by ____. It also helps us learn ____ so that ____. A ____ can help because ____. The national day on ____ provides time to ____. However, ____. Responsibility today can include ____.
Give one route per learner. Keep the structured answer in books, typed or exactly scribed as directed. The same common finish applies across routes, including the national day’s date and purpose from R5. The displayed model illustrates structure; it does not replace that required fact. Record the help actually used. Do not assess strength of emotion or participation in a public act as historical understanding.

slides.title: Check your explanation
slides.stage: Adult audience reply, one NS and learner response.

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: Have you explained remembrance of people, warning and responsibility?

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: Does your example show how a form helps, with a reason?

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: Have you included the day’s date and purpose, a limit and a safe action?

shapes.name: body-3
shapes.text: Hear or read one next step. Make your own response.

slides.notes:
Offer to the Communication portfolio. Record R only after the learner gives an idea, an adult audience replies with one NS (next step), and the learner responds in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. Record E only after actual banking. Keep the response mode and actual help. A partner answer does not establish both learners’ understanding.
Check whether the answer explains why remembering matters today, rather than only listing forms. A reason should connect people, warning or responsibility to significance. Include an example form, a limit and a safe present-day action. Respect different views about which form helps, provided reasons remain factual and respectful.

slides.title: Remembering with care today
slides.stage: Closing reflection on dignity, accurate learning and safe responsibility today.

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: One safe way to act with care is ____.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: Holocaust Memorial Day is tomorrow, 27 January.

shapes.name: body-3
shapes.text: You may respond privately or pass. No personal story or pledge is required.

slides.notes: Close with remembrance and responsibility today. Holocaust Memorial Day is 27 January, the day after this planned lesson. The national day’s purpose is discussed in general terms in the print pack. Do not introduce imagery, testimony, ceremony or a new live resource at the close. Passing and private responses remain available. A safe action can be checking a historical claim or seeking trusted adult help for hate. Do not promise that an individual action prevents genocide. Check readiness to leave.

slides.title: Words for remembrance

shapes.name: def-0
shapes.text: Taking time to remember people and learn from the past.

shapes.name: def-1
shapes.text: The worth of every person, deserving respect.

shapes.name: def-2
shapes.text: Something that helps us recognise a risk of harm.

shapes.name: def-3
shapes.text: What we should do with care for other people.

shapes.name: def-4
shapes.text: Why something matters, and to whom.

slides.notes: Available throughout, no additional minutes. Word help supports the enquiry, including significance as why something matters and to whom. Add relevant definitions from the printed word mat if asked. Plan in any language, use usual aids and read privately on request. Do not make knowledge of specialist terms a barrier to explaining a clear reason.

slides.title: Care and calm staff responses
slides.stage: Hidden adult care brief; no pupil time.

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: No imagery, testimony, victim roles or personal disclosure.

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: No forced grief, public acts or pledges. Calm factual responses count.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: Keep the supervised pause and neutral alternative available.

shapes.name: body-3
shapes.text: Stop antisemitism firmly. Reset respect after flippancy. Do not debate denial.

shapes.name: body-4
shapes.text: Record actual understanding, help and deferred work.

slides.notes:
This lesson is complete with the supplied text. Add no imagery or survivor testimony in any form: no quotation, paraphrase, invented voice, composite, audio, video or unplanned live browsing. The school’s chosen memorial-day resource may be reviewed privately by the teacher if the school approves, within the same care limits. No title, organisation or address is named here; no extra content is required.
Keep the dignity and full lives of people in view. Do not use imagine-you-are tasks, victim roles, historical role play, comparisons of suffering or personal family-history questions. Do not ask any learner to speak for Jewish people, survivors or a whole community. Do not invent a life story to make the topic feel personal.
Participation is thoughtful learning, not a performance of grief. Do not require a particular feeling, silence, prayer, pledge, public statement or personal disclosure. Quiet listening, private work and passing are allowed. Assess the explanation, not visible sadness or agreement with a ritual.
Agree a discreet PAUSE signal, supervising adult, quiet place and private return check before teaching. Keep both learners supervised. If a sole adult cannot supervise separate spaces, use a calm place in the room or pause the whole group while seeking usual support. Never send a learner away alone.
For distress, stop the demand, acknowledge it calmly and offer the agreed route without sanction or a public explanation. Do not probe or insist on a history recap while the learner is upset. Follow the school’s existing safeguarding arrangements for disclosures and use the appropriate private record.
Interrupt antisemitism calmly and firmly. Name the harm without repeating a slur. Hostility towards Jewish people is unacceptable. Correct a falsehood briefly and follow school procedures. Do not debate Holocaust denial or require learners to defend victims’ rights. Victims were not responsible for their persecution.
For flippancy or laughter, stop and reset respectful listening. A nervous response is possible, but harm still needs addressing. Follow up privately, check those affected and use existing procedures for targeted, repeated or serious incidents. Avoid shaming or guessing motives.
A warning is a reason to learn and act carefully, not a prediction that every unfair act leads to genocide. Do not equate everyday disagreement with the Holocaust. Remembrance alone cannot prevent hatred; education, laws, institutions and human choices matter too. Learners do not carry personal responsibility for preventing genocide.
Offer the neutral quiet task and a private readiness check. It is not evidence of the remembrance outcome. Record deferred work honestly and offer a later supported return. A partner’s answer or participation in a ceremony does not establish the learner’s understanding.
Quiet task: put these made-up daily times in order: 14:00 club; 08:30 reading; 12:00 lunch; 10:00 break. Copy or point to the first and last. Then sort pencil and book, cup and plate, by use. No history words or personal story are needed.
The owner’s strict care brief controls. All content is explanatory guidance, with no historical voice, survivor account, image, named organisation or website. Read Planner/Cover_Plan and Staff_Answers before delivery. The quiet alternative is not history evidence; record deferred work honestly.
